2. Remarks/Discussion of Issues
Claims
By the present Amendment, claims 23 and 32 are canceled, without prejudice and without disclaimer of the subject matter. Claims 16 and 24-30 have been revised, and new claims 34-36 have been submitted for consideration. No new matter is added. Claims 16-17, 19-22, 24-31 and 33-36 are pending in the application, which Applicant respectfully submits are in condition for allowance.
35 U.S. C. § 112(a) or 35 U.S. C. § 112, First Paragraph, Rejection
The Office Action rejects claims 16-17 and 19-33 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph, as assertedly failing to comply with the written description requirement. See Office Action, pp. 2-3.
The first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) and U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph provides: "The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention." To satisfy the written description requirement, the Specification as originally filed must provide sufficient detail for one skilled in the art to reasonably conclude that the inventors had possession of the claimed invention. See, e.g., Moba, B. V v. Diamond Automation, Inc., 325 F.3d 1306, 1319, 66 USPQ2d 1429, 1438 (Fed. Cir. 2003), cited by MPEP § 2163(I). Notably, "[t]here is a strong presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed." MPEP § 2163(I) (citing In re Wertheim, 541 F.2d 257, 263, 191 USPQ 90, 97 (CCPA 1976)) (emphasis added). Also, "[t]he examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in an applicant's disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims." See MPEP 2163.04 (citing In re Wertheim, 541 F.2d at 263, 191 USPQ at 97) (emphasis added).
Without acquiescing to the grounds of rejection, Applicant has revised claim 16, for example, to clarify that the instructions cause the computer to determine a plurality of curves defined by the bendable segment in the plurality of different arrangements of the bendable segment introduced within the cavity, respectively, using optical shape sensing information from the catheter, and that the plurality of curves comprise at least one contact curve corresponding to at least one respective arrangement of the plurality of different arrangements for which it is determined that the bendable segment is in contact with the inner wall of the cavity, and at least one non-contact curve corresponding to at least one respective arrangement of the plurality of different arrangements for which it is determined that the bendable segment is not in contact with the inner wall of the cavity. The Specification, as filed, provides abundant support for these features for one skilled in the art to reasonably conclude that the inventors had possession of the claimed invention. For example, the Specification discloses determining curves using optical shape sensing within the catheter, e.g., using optical fibers in. See, e.g., p. 6, lines 3-7; p. 10, lines 3-5; p. 11, lines 18-20; p. 12, line 27 - p. 13, line 6. The Specification also discloses determining whether a curve is a contact or non-contact curve, e.g., using electrodes. See, e.g., p. 8, line 27 - p. 9, line 27.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the Specification provides sufficient detail for one skilled in the art to reasonably conclude that the inventors had possession of the claimed invention, and thus requests withdrawal of the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph.
35 U.S.C. §101 Rejection
The Office Action rejects claims 16-17 and 19-33 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as assertedly being directed to non-statutory subject mater. See Office Action, p. 3-5. The Office Action asserts that the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea), and that the claims do not include additional elements that integrate the abstract ideal into a practical application, or amount to significantly more than the abstract idea. Id. In particular, the Office Action asserts that the claims fall within the "Mental Processes" grouping of abstract ideas. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection.
According to the United States Supreme Court in Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int'l, 573 U.S. 208, 134 S. Ct. 2347, 110 USPQ2d 1976 (2014), the determination of whether a claim is directed to patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 comprises a two-part analysis. First, it must be determined whether the claim is directed to a "patent-ineligible concept" (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, or physical phenomena). Second, if the claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept, it must be determined whether "an element or combination of elements that is 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself."' See, e.g., Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357, 110 USPQ2d at 1981.
The 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility, United States Patent and Trademark Office (December 16, 2014), provides a two-part analysis, after an initial step of determining whether the claim is directed to a processes, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, regarding how the Office determines whether a claim is directed toward section 101 patent-eligible subject matter. Interim Eligibility Guidance, Federal Register/Vol. 79, No. 241/Tuesday, December 16, 2014/Rules and Regulations, p. 74621. Thus, after first determining the first step (Step 1) of whether the claim is to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, one must perform the two part Alice analysis: (A) Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A), and (B) if an abstract idea is present in the claim, determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself (Step 2B). See also MPEP 2106(III).
With regard to Step 1, under 35 U.S.C. § 101, there are four categories of subject matter eligible for patent protection: (1) processes; (2) machines; (3) manufactures; and (4) compositions of matter. Claims 16, 17, 19-22, 26-31 and 33 are directed to machines or manufactures, and claims 24 and 25 are directed to processes, and therefore all claims fall within 35 U.S.C. § 101.
Step 2A addresses whether the method and article of manufacture are directed to an abstract idea. According to the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance, Step 2A is further divided into two prongs for determining whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception, including abstract ideas. In Prong One, it is determined whether the claim recites a judicial exception, and with regard to an abstract idea in particular, whether the claim recites subject matter from one of three groupings: (a) mathematical concepts, (b) certain methods of organizing human activity-fundamental economic principles or practices, and (c) mental processes. "Claims that do not recite matter that falls within these enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas ...." See Federal Register / Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 53. If it is determined that the claim does recite a judicial exception, then the analysis proceeds to Prong Two of Step 2A. In Prong Two, it is determined whether the recited judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea) is integrated into a practical application of that judicial exception. Id.
With regard to Prong One, the revised guidance for analyzing patentable subject matter provides: "Claims do not recite a mental process when they do not contain limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind, for instance when the human mind is not equipped to perform the claim limitations. See SRIInt'l, Inc. v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 930 F.3d 1295, 1304 (Fed. Cir. 2019) (declining to identify the claimed collection and analysis of network data as abstract because 'the human mind is not equipped to detect suspicious activity by using network monitors and analyzing network packets as recited by the claims')..." See MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(III)(A) (emphasis added).
Similarly, claim 16, for example, recites a memory storing instructions causing a computer to determine whether the bendable segment is in contact with an inner wall of the cavity in each arrangement of a plurality of different arrangements of the bendable segment introduced within the cavity. This is particularly the case where determining whether the bendable segment is in contact with the inner wall of the cavity includes receiving electrical signals from electrodes, arranged on the bendable segment, contacting the inner wall of the cavity. See claims 34-36. Also, claim 16 recites determining a plurality of curves defined by the bendable segment in the plurality of different arrangements of the bendable segment introduced within the cavity, respectively, using optical shape sensing information from the catheter, wherein the plurality of curves comprise at least one contact curve corresponding to at least one respective arrangement of the plurality of different arrangements for which it is determined that the bendable segment is in contact with the inner wall of the cavity, and at least one non-contact curve corresponding to at least one respective arrangement of the plurality of different arrangements for which it is determined that the bendable segment is not in contact with the inner wall of the cavity; and reconstructing the cavity, in response to the determined at least one contact curve and the at least one non-contact curve, to provide a map for guiding the catheter. Applicant therefore respectfully submits that these features cannot be performed in the human mind, and thus claim 16 is not directed to an abstract idea.
However, assuming arguendo that claim 16, recites at least one abstract idea, the question becomes whether that abstract idea is integrated into a practical application. "A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception." See Federal Register/Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 54 (emphasis added).
In the present Application, claim 16 integrates any potential abstract idea into at least the practical application of reconstructing the cavity, in response to the at least one contact curve and the at least one non-contact curve, to provide a map for guiding the catheter. This practical limitation prevents monopolization (improper pre-emption) of any potential abstract idea recited in claim 16, and therefore evidences a practical application of the same.
Another consideration indicative of an additional element integrating the judicial exception into a practical application is whether it reflects an improvement in the function of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or technical field. Id. In this context, the claimed embodiments result in improvements in the field of medical imaging, where a cavity (e.g., heart chamber) can be more quickly and effectively reconstructed using set of curves defined by a bendable segment of a catheter, as opposed to relying on points of contact by the distal tip of the catheter.
The Specification identifies the technical problem addressed by the claimed subject matter as: "Since in an acceptable time only few different positions of the tip of the ablation catheter within the cavity can be determined, the reconstructed cavity, which is determined based on only these few locations of the tip of the ablation catheter, has a poor quality only." See Specification, p. 1, lines 14-17.
The claimed subject matter provides an improvement in the technical field that addresses this technical problem: "It is an object of the present invention to provide a cavity determination apparatus, a cavity determination method and a cavity determination computer program for determining a cavity within an object, which allows determining the cavity within the object with improved quality in a relatively short time." See p. 1, lines 20-23 (emphasis added). In more detail:
The apparatus described above with reference to Figs. 1 and 2 is therefore preferentially adapted such that the positioning device can be replaced by a shape sensing device, which enables the reconstruction to be based on curves, rather than points, in a much faster fashion. In particular, shape sensing technology is preferentially used, in order to recover very quickly the shape of the cavity.... In particular, a catheter may be moved rapidly and in a more or less random fashion to quickly get the bulk of the cavity, for instance, of the left atrium of a heart of a person. The outcome of the corresponding algorithm can then be used as a rough map to guide the catheter into areas where the acquisition should be refined, for instance, because of a particularly high interest in this area and/or because the area is more difficult to access due to larger curvatures which could have hampered a correct acquisition during the initial sweep. Higher curvatures may be present, for instance, in pulmonary veins.
See p. 12, line 27 - p. 13, line 6 (emphasis added). See also p. 2, lines 1-13 ("Since not only single locations within the cavity are acquired, but curves defined by the bendable segment within the cavity in the different arrangements, a lot of spatial information can be acquired very fast. This allows reconstructing the cavity with improved quality in a relatively short time.") (emphasis added); p. 6, lines 3-7 ("The introduction element and the curve determination unit are preferentially adapted to determine the curves defined by the bendable segment within the cavity by optical shape sensing. This allows the apparatus to reliably determine the different curves defined by the bendable segment within the cavity, without necessarily requiring further localization units like an electromagnetic localization unit or an x-ray localization unit.") (emphasis added). Thus, claim 16 clearly is directed to improvements in other technology or technical field.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the claims also satisfy Prong Two in Step 2A of the analysis as set forth 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance. Therefore, the first part of the Alice analysis is satisfied, and the second part need not be addressed.
However, assuming arguendo that Step 2A has not been satisfied, Applicant proceeds to apply the second part of the Alice analysis (Step 2B). In accordance with Step 2B, Applicant submits that various elements in the claims are sufficient to ensure that the claims amount to significantly more than the abstract idea itself, particularly in that the claims as a whole is for a particular application of the asserted abstract idea. See, e.g., Federal Register/Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 56 ("[I]f a claim has been determined to be directed to a judicial exception under revised Step 2A, examiners should then evaluate the additional elements individually and in combination under Step 2B to determine whether they provide an inventive concept (i.e., whether the additional elements amount to significantly more than the exception itself.").
For example, claim 16 recites inter alia a catheter for being introduced into the cavity, wherein the catheter is shape sensing enabled and comprises a bendable segment for being arranged within the cavity in different arrangements, and in response to determinations of contact and non-contact curves, reconstruct the cavity to provide a map for guiding the catheter.
Accordingly, even assuming elements may involve abstract ideas, the claims are still directed to patent eligible subject matter due to application of the inventive concept. Applicant submits that the claims satisfy the second stage of the Alice Corp. test, and that the claims amount to significantly more than the abstract idea itself. See, e.g. Electric Power Group, LLC v. Alstom S.A., 830 F.3d 1350 (Fed. Cir. 2016) ("Reflecting those points, we have described ... the second-stage inquiry (where reached) as looking more precisely at what the claim elements add-specifically, whether, in the Supreme Court's terms, they identify an "'inventive concept"' in the application of the ineligible matter to which (by assumption at stage two) the claim is directed." (citing Enfish, LLC v. Microsoft Corp., 822 F.3d 1327, 1335-36 (Fed. Cir. 2016); Internet Patents Corp. v.
Active Network, Inc., 790 F.3d 1343, 1346 (Fed. Cir. 2015); Bascom GlobalInternet Servs., Inc. v. AT&TMobilityLLC, No. 2015-1763, 2016 WL 3514158, at *5 (Fed. Cir. June 27, 2016)).
Notably, the "inventive concept" that transforms the abstract idea into a patent- eligible invention "may arise in one or more of the individual claim limitations or in the ordered combination of the limitations," as discussed above. See BASCOM, at p. 13 (citing Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2355) (emphasis added). In addition, as discussed above in the analysis under Prong Two of revised Step 2A, the claim features recite improvements in other technology or technical field. Again, such improvements amount to "significantly more" than the assertedly abstract idea itself, transforming the abstract idea into a patent- eligible application. See, e.g., Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357, 110 USPQ2d at 1981 (Syllabus at 3, Slip Op. at 15). See also BASCOM, p. 17 ("Thus, construed in favor of the nonmovant -BASCOM the claims are 'more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the [abstract idea].' Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357. Instead, the claims may be read to "improve[] an existing technological process." Id. at 2358 (discussing the claims in Diehr, 450 U.S. 175)."). Accordingly, even assuming the claims are directed to abstract ideas, they still include patent eligible subject matter since they recite improvements to a technical field in accordance with the Alice analysis.
Accordingly, for at least the reasons set forth above, Applicant respectfully submits that the second part of the Alice test is also not satisfied, and therefore respectfully request withdrawal of the rejection of all pending claims under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
35 U.S.C. §102 Rejection
Claims 16-17, 19-22, 24-31 and 33 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) as being anticipated by Ben-Haim et al. (U.S. Patent No. 6,892,091). See Office Action, p. 6. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection at least for the reasons discussed below. Applicant's silence on certain aspects of the rejections is by no means a concession as to their propriety.
Claim 1
In rejecting claim 1, the Office Action asserts that "a catheter for being introduced into the cavity, wherein the catheter is shape sensing enabled and comprises a bendable segment for being arranged within the cavity in different arrangements" is disclosed by catheter 20; col. 10, lines 59-67; that "a computer including a non-transitory storage medium for storing instructions" is disclosed by computer 36; col. 8, lines 10-15; that "determine whether the bendable segment is in contact with an inner wall of the cavity in each arrangement of a plurality of different arrangements of the bendable segment introduced within the cavity" is disclosed by col. 11, lines 35-67, col. 12, lines 1-28; that "determine at least one contact curve defined by the bendable segment in each arrangement of the bendable segment determined to be in contact with the inner wall of the cavity" is disclosed by FIGs. 3a-3c; col. 9, line 25; col. 13, lines 37-67; col. 11, lines 35-67; col. 12, lines 1-28; via electrodes 24, 45; that "determine at least one non-contact curve defined by the bendable segment in each arrangement of the bendable segment determined not to be in contact with the inner wall of the cavity" is disclosed by col. 9, lines 57-67; col. 10, lines 1-40; col. 11, lines 35-67; col. 12, lines 1-28; via non-contact electrodes 25; that "using shape sensing information from the catheter, wherein each curve is defined by an introduction of the bendable segment within the cavity in the respective arrangement of the plurality of different arrangements" is disclosed by FIG. 6; col. 9, lines 45-50; col. 12, lines 1-28; that "reconstruct the cavity" is disclosed by col. 12, lines 5-12; and that "in response to the determined at least one contact curve and the at least one non-contact curve, to provide a map for guiding the catheter" is disclosed by col. 9, line 25; col. 11, lines 35-67, col 12, lines 1-28; col. 13, lines 37-67, of Ben-Haim et al. See Office Action, pp. 6-7.
Without acquiescing to the grounds of rejection, Applicant has revised claim 16 inter alia to clarify that the instructions cause the computer to determine a plurality of curves defined by the bendable segment in the plurality of different arrangements of the bendable segment introduced within the cavity, respectively, using optical shape sensing information from the catheter, wherein the plurality of curves comprise at least one contact curve corresponding to at least one respective arrangement of the plurality of different arrangements for which it is determined that the bendable segment is in contact with the inner wall of the cavity, and at least one non-contact curve corresponding to at least one respective arrangement of the plurality of different arrangements for which it is determined that the bendable segment is not in contact with the inner wall of the cavity, as discussed above.
Ben-Haim et al. does not disclose determining a plurality of curves defined by the bendable segment in different arrangements. Rather, Ben-Haim et al. discloses identifying a first contact point 70 and a second contact point 72 where catheter tip 26 of catheter 20 contacts wall 68 of heart chamber 66 via contact electrode 24 at different locations. While the catheter 20 is in contact with the wall 68 at these locations, an array 23 of non-contact electrodes 25 are used to detect electrical information for generating an electrical map of the heart chamber 66. See, e.g., Ben-Haim et al., FIGs. 7A, 7B; col. 11, lines 33-60. There is no disclosure of actually determining curves of the catheter 20 in the different locations, and there is no apparent need to do so.
Further, even if Ben-Haim et al. did disclose determining curves, there is no disclosure of doing so using optical shape sensing information, as recited in claim 16. Simply, there is no disclosure whatsoever by Ben-Haim et al. of optical shape sensing, or using shape sensing in particular to determine curves defined by a bendable segment in different arrangements. Also, Ben-Haim et al. emphasizes reliance on using individual points to produce the electrical map, not curves (shape sensed or otherwise): "Briefly, in preferred embodiments of the present invention, a processor reconstructs a map, preferably a 3-D map, of the cardiac chamber from a plurality of sampled points on the chamber whose position coordinates have been determined." See col. 13, lines 27-32 (emphasis added). This fits squarely within the art over which claim 16 is an improvement. See, e.g., Specification, p. 12, lines 27-30 ("The apparatus described above with reference to Figs. 1 and 2 is therefore preferentially adapted such that the positioning device can be replaced by a shape sensing device, which enables the reconstruction to be based on curves, rather than points, in a much faster fashion.") (emphasis added).
In addition, even if Ben-Haim et al. did disclose determining curves using optical shape sensing information, none of these curves would be non-contact curves because all measurements are being made while the contact electrode 24 is in contact with the wall 68. See, e.g., col 11, lines 46-60 ("After the above electrical and location information is collected at first contact point 70, contact electrode 24 at the catheter tip 26 is advanced to a second contact point on the chamber surface. FIG. 7B shows the contact electrode 24 in contact with second contact point 72 on chamber wall 68.... Once again, contact electrode 24 is maintained in contact with wall 68 at contact point 72 throughout at least an entire cardiac cycle, during which time location information is measured by the location sensors, and electrical information is measured by contact electrode 24 and by each of the non-contact electrodes 25.") (emphasis added).
For anticipation, there must be no difference between the claimed invention and the reference disclosure, as viewed by a person of ordinary skill in the field of the invention. See, e.g., Scripps Clinic & Res. Found. v. Genentech, Inc., 927 F.2d 1565, 18 USPQ2d 1001 (Fed. Cir. 1991). Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that Ben- Haim et al. does not disclose each and every element of claim 16, and thus the rejection of claim 16 as being anticipated by Ben-Haim et al. under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) should be withdrawn.
Claim 24 and 26
Applicant respectfully submits that Ben-Haim et al. does not disclose each and every element of independent claims 24 and 26 for at least substantially the same reasons as claim 16, discussed above, and thus the rejection of claims 24 and 26 as being anticipated by Ben-Haim et al. under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) should be withdrawn.
Claims 17, 19-22, 25, 27-31 and 33
Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections of claims 17, 19-22, 25, 27-31 and 33, and submits that these claims are allowable over the applied art at least because they ultimately depend from independent claims 16, 24 and 26, respectively, which have been shown to be allowable over the applied art, as well as in view of their additional recitations. Accordingly, for the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the rejections of claims 17, 19-22, 25, 27-31 and 33 under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
New Claims
Applicant respectfully submits that new claims 34-36 are allowable over the applied art at least because they ultimately depend from independent claims 16, 24 and 26, respectively, which have been shown to be allowable over the applied art, as well as in view of their additional recitations. No new matter is added.
Rejections under 35 U.S.C. §103
Claims 23 and 32 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103(a) as being unpatentable over Ben-Haim et al. in view of Barbagli et al. (U. S. Patent No. 2009/0076476). See Office Action, p. 11. Without acquiescing to the propriety of the proposed combination of references, Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections, and submits that claims 23 and 32 are allowable over the applied art at least because they ultimately depend from independent claims 16 and 26, respectively, which have been shown to be allowable, as well as in view of their additional recitations. Thus, withdrawal of the rejections of claims 23 and 32 is respectfully requested.
Conclusion
In view of the foregoing explanations, Applicant respectfully requests that theExaminer reconsider and reexamine the present application, allow claims 16-17, 19-22,24-31 and 36, and pass the application to issue. In the event that there are any outstandingmatters remaining in the present application, the Examiner is invited to contact Van C.Ernest (Reg. No. 44,099) at (571) 283.0720 to discuss these matters.
